title: Imports and Namespace
content: Imports Mathlib's prime number basics, GCD, Finset operations, and general tactics. The Finset.Ico (interval, closed-open) is the key data structure for representing integer intervals [a, b). The namespace Erdos1056 isolates all definitions.
mathContext: The formalization builds on $\texttt{Finset.Ico}\;a\;b = \{a, a+1, \ldots, b-1\}$, the discrete closed-open interval. Products over $\texttt{Ico}$ give interval products $\prod_{i=a}^{b-1} i$.

title: Interval Product
content: The product of all integers in the half-open interval [a, b), defined as the Finset product of the identity function over Finset.Ico a b. When a >= 1, this equals b!/a!. The condition intervalProd a b % p = 1 means the interval is 'multiplicatively trivial' modulo p.
mathContext: $\text{intervalProd}(a, b) = \prod_{i \in \text{Ico}(a,b)} i = \prod_{i=a}^{b-1} i$. For $a \ge 1$: $\text{intervalProd}(a,b) = b!/a!$. The congruence $\text{intervalProd}(a,b) \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ is equivalent to $a! \equiv b! \pmod{p}$, connecting interval products to factorial residues.

title: Valid Boundary Sequence
content: A valid boundary for k intervals is a list of k+1 strictly increasing natural numbers. The strict monotonicity (via List.Chain') ensures each interval [a_i, a_{i+1}) is non-empty, so every interval has a well-defined non-trivial product.
mathContext: $\text{IsValidBoundary}(\text{boundaries}, k) \iff |\text{boundaries}| = k+1 \land a_0 < a_1 < \cdots < a_k$. The strict ordering ensures each interval $[a_i, a_{i+1})$ contains at least one integer.

title: All Products Congruent to One
content: The combined condition: valid boundaries AND every interval product is congruent to 1 modulo p. Uses Fin k to index into the k intervals, accessing boundaries at positions i and i+1. This is the core predicate that verified examples must satisfy.
mathContext: $\text{AllProductsCongruentOne}(p, [a_0, \ldots, a_k], k) \iff \text{valid boundaries} \land \forall j \in \{0, \ldots, k-1\},\; \prod_{i=a_j}^{a_{j+1}-1} i \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$

title: Solution Existence Predicate
content: HasSolution k asserts: there exists a prime p and a list of boundaries such that all k interval products are congruent to 1 modulo p. This is the central predicate of the formalization. Proving HasSolution k for specific k values is the verified content; the open conjecture is that HasSolution k holds for ALL k >= 2.
mathContext: $\text{HasSolution}(k) \iff \exists p \text{ prime},\; \exists a_0 < \cdots < a_k,\; \forall j,\; \prod_{i=a_j}^{a_{j+1}-1} i \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Equivalently: $\exists p$ prime with $k+1$ values whose factorials agree modulo $p$.

title: Infrastructure Lemmas
content: Five proved lemmas supporting the main theorems: (1) intervalProd_empty: empty intervals have product 1; (2-4) IsValidBoundary helpers extracting length, chain, and count properties; (5) intervalProd_pos: products are positive when starting at >= 1; (6) mod_mul_of_mod_eq_one: products of congruent-to-1 values remain congruent to 1. These establish the basic algebraic and structural properties needed for the verified examples.
mathContext: Key results: $\prod_{i=a}^{b-1} i = 1$ when $b \le a$ (empty product), and $a \equiv 1, b \equiv 1 \pmod{p} \implies ab \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ (closure of the trivial residue class under multiplication). The positivity lemma $\text{intervalProd}(a,b) > 0$ for $a \ge 1, a < b$ ensures interval products are meaningful natural numbers.

title: Erdos k=2 Solution (p=11)
content: Verified proof that HasSolution 2 holds, using p=11 with boundaries [3, 5, 8]. The two intervals are [3,5) = {3,4} with product 12 and [5,8) = {5,6,7} with product 210. Both 12 % 11 = 1 and 210 % 11 = 1. The proof unfolds all definitions and uses fin_cases with native_decide for computational verification.
mathContext: Erdos (1979): $p = 11$, boundaries $[3, 5, 8]$. Interval $[3,5)$: $3 \cdot 4 = 12 = 11 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$. Interval $[5,8)$: $5 \cdot 6 \cdot 7 = 210 = 19 \cdot 11 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$. In factorial form: $2! = 2$, $4! = 24 \equiv 2$, $7! = 5040 \equiv 2 \pmod{11}$.

title: Makowski k=3 Solution (p=17)
content: Verified proof that HasSolution 3 holds, using p=17 with boundaries [2, 6, 12, 16]. Three intervals: [2,6) with product 120, [6,12) with product 332640, [12,16) with product 32760. All congruent to 1 modulo 17. The proof structure mirrors erdos_k2 with one additional fin_cases branch.

title: Combined Known Solutions
content: Bundles the k=2 and k=3 results into a conjunction (known_small_solutions) and proves problem non-triviality by exhibiting a specific k >= 2 with a solution. These serve as the verified foundation for the open conjecture.
mathContext: $\text{HasSolution}(2) \land \text{HasSolution}(3)$, and $\exists k \ge 2,\; \text{HasSolution}(k)$. The conjunction confirms both known cases, while the existential witnesses that the conjecture is non-vacuously satisfiable.

title: Known Solutions Use Odd Primes
content: Both verified solutions use odd primes (11 and 17, both > 2). This is expected: for p=2, intervalProd a b % 2 = 1 requires an odd product, but consecutive integers alternate parity, making solutions impossible for even-length intervals. The odd prime constraint is likely necessary for all solutions.
mathContext: For $p = 2$: $\prod_{i=a}^{b-1} i \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$ requires all factors odd, impossible for consecutive integers when $b - a \ge 2$. Thus solutions require $p > 2$, i.e., odd primes. Both known solutions ($p = 11, 17$) satisfy $p > 2$.

title: Wilson's Theorem for p=11 and p=17
content: Computationally verified instances of Wilson's theorem for the two primes used in known solutions: (10)! % 11 = 10 and (16)! % 17 = 16. These confirm that (p-1)! = p-1 (mod p), which equals -1 (mod p). Proved by native_decide.
mathContext: $10! = 3628800 \equiv 10 \pmod{11}$ and $16! = 20922789888000 \equiv 16 \pmod{17}$. In both cases $(p-1)! \equiv p-1 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$, confirming Wilson's theorem for the specific primes in the known solutions.

title: General Wilson's Theorem Constraint
content: States Wilson's theorem in general: for any prime p, the product of [1, p) equals p-1 modulo p. Declared as an axiom since the general proof requires Mathlib's Wilson's theorem infrastructure. This is the key structural constraint: if k intervals with product 1 partitioned {1,...,p-1}, the total product would be 1^k = 1 != -1 (mod p), a contradiction.
mathContext: **Wilson's theorem** (axiomatized): $\forall p$ prime, $\prod_{i=1}^{p-1} i \equiv p - 1 \pmod{p}$, i.e., $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$. **Consequence**: if $k$ intervals partition $\{1, \ldots, p-1\}$ with each product $\equiv 1$, then $(p-1)! \equiv 1^k = 1 \pmod{p}$, contradicting $-1 \ne 1$ for $p > 2$. So solutions must leave gaps.

title: Main Conjecture: All k >= 2
content: The core open problem stated as an axiom: for every k >= 2, HasSolution k. This claims that arbitrarily many consecutive intervals with products congruent to 1 modulo some prime always exist. Only k=2 and k=3 are verified. No k=4 solution is known, and exhaustive searches for small primes have not found one.
mathContext: **Erdos Problem #1056** (axiomatized): $\forall k \ge 2,\; \text{HasSolution}(k)$. Equivalently: for every $k \ge 2$, there exists a prime $p$ with $k+1$ values $q_0 < q_1 < \cdots < q_k < p$ satisfying $q_0! \equiv q_1! \equiv \cdots \equiv q_k! \pmod{p}$. **Status: OPEN.**

title: Noll-Simmons Factorial Generalization
content: Generalizes the conjecture: for every k, there exist a prime p and k values q_1 < ... < q_k < p with q_1! = ... = q_k! (mod p). This drops the 'consecutive intervals' structure, asking only for factorial collisions. The interval product conjecture implies Noll-Simmons (take q_i = a_i), but Noll-Simmons could be easier since it removes the consecutiveness constraint.
mathContext: **Noll-Simmons conjecture** (axiomatized): $\forall k,\; \exists p$ prime, $\exists Q : \text{Fin}\;k \to \mathbb{N}$, $(\forall i,\; Q(i) < p) \land (\forall i\;j,\; Q(i)! \equiv Q(j)! \pmod{p})$. This is weaker than Erdos #1056 since consecutive intervals give factorial collisions but not vice versa. The factorial function $n \mapsto n! \bmod p$ takes $p$ values in $\{0, \ldots, p-1\}$; by pigeonhole, some collisions must occur, but the question is whether the maximum collision multiplicity grows without bound.

title: Comprehensive Summary Theorem
content: Bundles all verified results into one conjunction: HasSolution 2, HasSolution 3, Wilson constraint for p=11, and Wilson constraint for p=17. This serves as the single 'deliverable' of the formalization, packaging the two verified examples alongside the Wilson's theorem confirmations that constrain the solution structure.
mathContext: $\text{HasSolution}(2) \land \text{HasSolution}(3) \land (10! \equiv 10 \pmod{11}) \land (16! \equiv 16 \pmod{17})$. The conjunction packages the complete verified content of the formalization.
